AI is rapidly rewriting the process and paperwork layer for Postal Service Clerks, but on-site judgment and professional experience still rest with people. This article breaks down the specific impact and how to respond.
It does not suit people who dislike repetition, cannot remain at a window, or cannot tolerate queues. The work frequently brings urgency and complaints, making carelessness difficult.

A common path is: start as a counter clerk → work at a comprehensive service window → independently handle complex transactions → manage branch back-office work → become a branch director or move into management.
This work suits careful, steady people who follow procedures and serve the public. If error-free work is your standard, you can build a stable career here.

Postal service clerks handle mailing, stamps, money orders, registered-mail tracking, and other public transactions at post-office counters, operate dedicated systems, and ensure accurate, compliant service.

paragraphs: At the start of a shift, open the counter, count assets, and log in to systems. During the morning, process mailing, sell stamps, and answer inquiries without interruption. Around midday, reconcile accounts and complete missing forms. In the afternoon, handle registered mail, money orders, and difficult items and reassure complaining customers. Before leaving, balance documents and cash and prepare for the next day.

In short: align mail with the system at the counter. Tasks include accepting and mailing items, selling stamps, processing money orders, tracking and redemption, and answering inquiries. It uses both hands and speech on the front line of postal service.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 74,200 postal service clerks were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to fall to 71,600 by 2034, a net loss of about 2,600 jobs, with about 6,100 openings annually and a 2026 median annual salary of about $61,600 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace postal clerks, but it will reduce routine business. Self-service terminals and online systems accelerate mailing and tracking, shifting clerks from standard transactions toward identity verification, complex items, service for older customers, and counter management. People limited to routine entry will be displaced, while those who understand rules and serve well are more secure.
A 5/10 places this occupation in a moderately AI-exposed field. Routine transactions accelerate, but verification and service still require people.

Moderate-to-high exposure does not mean high risk. What gets replaced is entering standard forms, not verification and service roles. People who serve well and understand rules become scarcer as self-service spreads. Those limited to routine entry face the greatest risk.
This is a stable entry path, but pure data entry is shrinking in the AI era, so develop service and verification skills early.
Advance from handling transactions to counter management + difficult customer service, and learn systems and rules.
Emphasize accuracy and patience, and specify the transaction types you have handled.
Hire for steadiness and service orientation. Core staff who can run a counter are worth retaining.

No matter how smart terminals become, clerks still verify identities, resolve difficult items, and reassure customers. People cannot be removed completely from the service window.
In short, the future shortage will not be of people who can enter forms, but of postal clerks who understand rules, verify accurately, and serve well.
